newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan minister cleared in murder of tourist Ward.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan minister cleared in murder of tourist Ward.

text.p: Kenyan authorities on Tuesday cleared cabinet minister Nicholas Biwott and President Daniel arap Moi's son Jonathan Toroitich of involvement in the 1988 murder in a Kenyan game reserve of British tourist Julie Ward.
Attorney-General Amos Wako told reporters an inquiry team had also cleared Criminal Investigations Department Director Noah arap Too and seven others of involvement in the murder.
Wako said a Kenyan witness exiled in Denmark, Valentinus Kodipo, had made "serious allegations of complicity" in the murder of Julie Ward against Biwott, Toroitich, Too and the others.
Biwott is a minister of state at the presidency responsible for regional cooperation. In 1988, he was energy minister.

Biwott returned to the cabinet in January after being removed in 1991 as industry minister after allegations of corruption against him at a judicial inquiry into the 1990 murder of foreign minister Robert Ouko.
British detectives had named Biwott and former senior civil servant Hezekiah Anguka as prime suspects in Ouko's murder.
Biwott has vehemently denied any involvement in the death.
Wako's news conference in Nairobi was attended by Julie Ward's father John Ward, who said he was confident of a "logical conclusion" to the case after a last lead was checked.

Wako said all but one lead in the case had been investigated and had not shed any new light. He said the findings on the one remaining lead would be handed over to him by June 30 after which he would decide whether to prosecute any suspect.
John Ward said of the remaining lead: "Certain matters have occurred recently leading to a logical progression of events. I am optimistic that we will reach a logical conclusion."
"I fully agree with the investgations so far. I also wanted this interim report so these public figures could be cleared at the earliest opportunity," the hotelier said.

Julie Ward's mutilated remains were discovered in 1988 in a remote corner of the world-famous Masai Mara game reserve, 200 km (125 miles) south of the capital. Two game rangers charged with the murder were acquitted in 1992 for lack of evidence.
Kenyan police initially said Julie Ward, 28, was killed by animals but a judge said police had callously attempted to cover up the killing.

John Ward has spent a personal fortune of $760,000 in a search for Julie's killers and is still seeking compensation from the Kenyan government -- partly based on the trial judge's observations on how police had originally conducted the case.
